# Exact divisors of the odd coefficient sum at both power indices

<a id="statement"></a>
## Divisibility in the order generated by a unit root

Let \(|a|=q,\ |b|=q+1\) with \(q\ge1\), take coprime integers \(0<u<v\), and put \(\epsilon=\pm1\).
Suppose \(\beta\) is a nontorsion algebraic unit root of the [reciprocal section](Yin_C_G0345_v869.md#statement)
\[
 a(1+\epsilon X^{u+v})+b(X^u+\epsilon X^v).
\]
This includes the primitive power \(\beta=z^g\) of any nontorsion unit root at a common dilation \(g\ge1\).
Write \(A=\mathbb Z[\beta]\), let \(S\) be the monic minimal polynomial of \(\beta\), set \(D=\deg S\), and take norms from \(\mathbb Q(\beta)\) to \(\mathbb Q\).
Define
\[
 L=2q+1,\qquad s=\operatorname{sgn}(b/a),\qquad t=-\epsilon s,
 \qquad T=s\beta^u,\qquad Z=t\beta^v,\qquad
 U_n=\frac{\beta^{2n}-1}{\beta^2-1}.
\]
The elements \(U_u,U_v\) generate the unit ideal in \(A\) and their product divides \(L\) in \(A\).
In particular every prime ideal of the ring of integers that divides \(\beta^{2n}-1\), for \(n=u\) or \(v\), lies over \(L\) or divides \(\beta^2-1\).
At primes away from \(L\) the valuation of \(\beta^{2n}-1\) equals that of \(\beta^2-1\) for both indices.
No prime ideal divides both quotients, even over \(L\).

Set \(E=qT+q+1\).
Then \(|N(E)|\mid L^u\), and whenever \(D\ge2u\) one has the integer divisibilities
\[
               L^{D-2u}\mid |N(U_v)|,\qquad
               |N(U_u)N(U_v)|\mid L^D.
\]
In particular every rational prime \(p\mid L\) occurs in \(N(U_v)\) when \(D>2u\).
For prime \(v\ne p\) this requires \(\operatorname{ord}_v(p)\le D\).
These conclusions apply to unrestricted exponents.
Their use to exclude individual parameter choices leaves open the existence of unit roots as \(q\to\infty\).

The ideal generated by \(1-Z\) alone equals \((1-Z,1-T)\) in \(A\).
If \(s^v=t^u\), there is a sign \(\eta\) with \(\eta^u=s,\ \eta^v=t\), and this ideal is \((1-\eta\beta)\).
In particular \((1-Z)/(1-\eta\beta)\) is a unit of \(A\) and \(|N(1-Z)|=|S(\eta)|\).
If \(s^v\ne t^u\), the ideal is \((2,1-\beta)\) and \(|N(1-Z)|=\gcd(2,|S(1)|)\).

<a id="quotients"></a>
## The section and its inverse

The section reads \(EZ=q+(q+1)T\).
Subtracting the two sides from \(E\) and adding them to \(E\) gives
\[
 E(1-Z)=1-T,\qquad E(1+Z)=L(1+T).
\]
Also \(E'=q+1-qZ\) belongs to \(A\), and substitution of \(EZ\) shows that \(EE'=L\).
Multiplying the two binomial identities and using \(T^2=\beta^{2u},\ Z^2=\beta^{2v}\) therefore yields
\[
 E^2U_v=L U_u,\qquad (E')^2U_u=L U_v.
\]
All displayed factors are nonzero because \(\beta\) is nontorsion and \(L>0\).

For \(G_n(X)=1+X+\cdots+X^{n-1}\), the subtraction \(G_n-X^{n-m}G_m=G_{n-m}\) when \(n>m>0\) gives \((G_u,G_v)=(G_1)=(1)\) in \(\mathbb Z[X]\) by the Euclidean algorithm on indices.
Evaluation at \(\beta^2\) gives \((U_u,U_v)=A\).
The two identities for their multiples now show \(U_v\mid L\) and \(U_u\mid L\), respectively.
Their comaximality implies \(U_uU_v\mid L\) in \(A\).
Extending the ideals to the full ring of integers and using \(\beta^{2n}-1=(\beta^2-1)U_n\) proves the valuation assertions.

<a id="norm"></a>
## The norm at every prime of the coefficient sum

Use \(E(X)=qsX^u+q+1\) and the integral parent \(F(X)=tX^vE(X)-q-(q+1)sX^u\).
At each root of \(E(X)\) one has \(F(X)=L/q\), so the absolute resultant of \(E(X)\) and \(F(X)\) is \(q^{u+v}(L/q)^u=q^v L^u\).
The monic \(S\) divides \(F\) in \(\mathbb Z[X]\), and multiplicativity of the resultant gives \(|N(E)|\mid q^vL^u\).
On the other hand \(EE'=L\) gives \(|N(E)|\mid L^D\).
Since \(q\) and \(L\) are coprime, \(|N(E)|\mid L^u\).
Taking norms in \(E^2 U_v=L U_u\) gives
\[
       |N(U_v)|=\frac{L^D |N(U_u)|}{|N(E)|^2}.
\]
This proves the lower divisibility when \(D\ge2u\), and taking norms in \(U_uU_v\mid L\) gives the upper divisibility.
The [primitive degree bound](Yin_C_G0345_v869.md#statement) ensures \(D>2u\) for all sufficiently large \(q\) in any sequence of unit roots.
For \(p\mid L\) and \(D>2u\), some prime ideal over \(p\) divides \(U_v\).
If \(v\) is prime and \(p\ne v\), the reduction of \(\beta^2\) at that ideal has order \(v\), since it is a root of \(G_v\) and \(G_v(1)=v\ne0\) in characteristic \(p\).
Its residue degree is at most \(D\), proving the stated order restriction.

<a id="signed"></a>
## The signed binomial ideal

Since \(E(1-Z)=1-T\), the ideal \(I=(1-Z,1-T)\) is generated by \(1-Z\).
If \(s^v=t^u\), take integers \(h,j\) with \(hu+jv=1\) and set \(\eta=s^h t^j\).
Then \(\eta^u=s,\ \eta^v=t\), and \(\eta\beta=T^h Z^j\) equals one modulo \(I\), since \(T\) and \(Z\) are units in \(A\).
Conversely both generators of \(I\) are multiples of \(1-\eta\beta\), so these principal ideals agree.
The nonzero generators differ by a unit, and the asserted norm follows from the minimal polynomial.

If \(s^v\ne t^u\), then \(T^v=-Z^u\), so \(2\in I\).
Modulo two the signs disappear, and \(\beta^u=\beta^v=1\) modulo \(I\) implies \(\beta=1\) there by the same Bézout identity.
Thus \((2,1-\beta)\subseteq I\), and the opposite inclusion follows by reducing both generators of \(I\) modulo \((2,1-\beta)\).
The presentation \(A=\mathbb Z[X]/(S)\) gives \(A/I=\mathbb Z/(2,S(1))\).
Multiplication by \(1-Z\) on the free additive group \(A\) has determinant \(N(1-Z)\), whose absolute value is the index of \(I\).
This gives the claimed norm also when \(I=A\).
